snippet.title: Popper Longplay (Arcade Game)
snippet.description:
- Popper Longplay (Arcade Game) -

Popper is a platform-action game developed and published by Omori Electric and released in arcades in 1983. Licensed to Alway Electronic Components for distribution in the United States, it stars a small rabbit hopping around geometric playfields while changing panels and avoiding enemies.

The influence of Q*bert is impossible to miss. Both games revolve around moving across elevated surfaces and altering panels by stepping on them, but Popper does more than simply recreate the famous pyramid with a different character. Its stages vary considerably in structure, giving the game a slightly broader arcade feel than its obvious inspiration.

The main objective is to cover the required panels by jumping across them while avoiding the creatures occupying the playfield. Falling from the edge costs a life, so movement has to be deliberate, particularly on the pseudo-3D stages where judging the correct direction can be surprisingly tricky.

Later rounds make the panel-clearing objective more demanding. Some tiles need to be stepped on more than once, while certain enemies can undo the player's work by changing completed panels back again. What begins as a straightforward exercise in covering the board therefore becomes increasingly difficult to keep under control.

Power-ups occasionally appear and temporarily allow the rabbit to defeat enemies rather than simply avoid them. This provides some welcome relief when the screen becomes crowded and also adds a more aggressive element that separates Popper from the purely evasive style normally associated with this type of game.

The game alternates between several kinds of stage rather than endlessly repeating one layout. Alongside the pseudo-3D sections are flatter water-based screens and bonus rounds, helping to keep the visual and mechanical rhythm from becoming too predictable. The bonus stages involve collecting bubbles within a time limit, with additional rewards available for surviving the entire sequence.

The controls are simple, but the movement has its own learning curve. Because the stages are presented from unusual perspectives, pushing in what seems like the obvious direction does not always produce the result expected. Once the movement becomes familiar, however, the game develops a pleasant rhythm of hopping, planning routes and reacting to enemies before they interfere with the panel pattern.

Popper never came remotely close to Q*bert's fame, and its similarities undoubtedly contributed to it being seen as another game following an already successful formula. Yet the comparison does not necessarily work against it. There is more variety here than its reputation might suggest, with different stage types, power-ups and changing objectives giving it a personality of its own.

For some reason, I actually find Popper more appealing than Q*bert. It may lack the iconic character design and historical importance of Gottlieb's classic, but I enjoy the additional variety and the slightly less rigid feel of its stages. It is derivative without being completely redundant, and once the controls click, there is a surprisingly enjoyable arcade game underneath its obvious inspiration.
